To address this issue, our novel Design Flow for Efficient Integrated Cryptography (DFEIC) streamlines the integration of cryptographic functions using lookup table-based neural networks. By aligning the dimensions of neural networks with hardware acceleration, DFEIC reduces memory usage and increases processing efficiency. Utilizing the design flow, we created three models: an efficient neural network for the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES-NET), a neural network for AES encryption (AES-NN), and a combined model that includes both data and target information. The results showed that AES-NN, with a latency of 157 clock cycles and a throughput of 10.8 Mbps, achieves comparable performance to AES-Accel, while requiring significantly less memory (2.5% of the original size). Furthermore, AES-NN demonstrates robust resistance to annealing noise, an issue commonly faced in quantum computing. Additionally, AES-NN has a relatively modest 384-bit memory footprint and can be trained using a relatively small dataset of 5120 entries after the initial training, which takes approximately 4 hours. The memory-efficient design and robustness of AES-NN make it an excellent choice for secure and efficient ANN implementations. The code for AES-NN has been made publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/yinghbih/AES-NN). The standard approach of relying solely on the checkpoint file leads to model drift, where the provided parameters no longer reflect the current model performance. The lack of explicit evaluation prompts prevents us from confidently using PLMs in new scenarios. To address these issues, we propose an efficient evaluation framework consisting of a subset of the original training data and a set of task-agnostic evaluation prompts. SSP) is a classic optimization task 
  that models a flexible manufacturing system with multiple interconnected production 
  stations. In this problem, a set of tasks is given, and the goal is to sequence 
  them across the stations while adhering to predetermined processing and transfer 
  time constraints. The problem's solution must be completed within a predefined time 
  frame, and there is a limit on the number of stations that can be occupied at any 
  given moment. Unlike traditional scheduling problems, DJSSP tasks are not predetermined, 
  as the problem includes an additional component where tasks must be selected from 
  a pool with unknown properties. This component is represented as a bipartite discrete 
  linear exclusion problem, which can be solved using a random discrete linear exclusion 
  algorithm, providing an approximate solution to the job-shop scheduling problem. 
  Our main contribution is a random discrete linear exclusion algorithm for solving 
  the dynamic job-shop scheduling problem when the system has two stations. 
  We prove that under certain conditions, this algorithm yields solutions that minimize 
  the makespan (the maximum completion time of any job) with a factor of $5.5$, 
  which is the first known performance guarantee for an approximation algorithm 
  for this specific problem instance. 
  Furthermore, we derive an estimate of the algorithm's expected makespan 
  as $O(9.5\tau)$, where $\tau$ is a parameter characterizing the complexity 
  of the problem instance, and also establish connections with other optimization 
  problems, offering implications for their approximation as well as providing 
  new insights for future research in this area.

These spots are not stationary and have been observed to move over the course of 13 days of observation as the star rotates on its axis. The speed at which these spots move on the surface of the star can be used to determine its rotational period and density, and with mass and radius already known, we were able to calculate its moment of inertia. We also found that the emission spots are associated with particular magnetic field patterns and that the emission spots move in tandem with the magnetic field as it rotates on the star. We were also able to compare the distribution of emission on the surface of K2-IIIe to the distribution of emission on the surface of the sun through the optical diagnosis technique, but found that the emission line emission from the surface of K2-IIIe is much more intense and has a broader spectral line profile than the emission from the surface of the sun. We also conclude that the optical diagnosing technique provides a direct view of the photospheric and chromospheric activity of a star. While chiral crystallography can identify the true handedness of invertsymmetric crystals, it requires the use of a right-handed spiral conveyor belt diagram known as the Friedel-Grafton method or a similar right-handed closure operation in other approaches. A question remains regarding the inherent handedness of these mathematical tools, as they can alternatively be constructed with a left-handed spiral conveyor belt. This inquiry prompts an examination of the fundamental principles of inversion symmetry, leading to the discovery that the central point of an inversion operation can be defined differently, depending on whether you consider the individual lattice sites or the connections between them. This distinction reveals the possibility of left-handed or right-handed inversion symmetry within the crystal structure itself, distinct from any external handedness induced by the choice of a particular crystallographic direction. This concept can be quantified through the use of the left- or right-handed cross product of lattice vectors, leading to the emergence of right- or left-handed crystalline helices that can occupy the same reciprocal space as their corresponding right- or left-handed protein folds. This finding implies that the handedness of crystalline helices or, more generally, the intrinsic handedness of inversion symmetric crystals, can be derivations from the Bragg reflection conditions that are potentially relevant to the direct observation of handedness in X-ray crystallography. This discovery can be particularly significant for the analysis of left-handed amino acids or other left-handed molecular components within the crystal structure. Moreover, this research implies that some left-handed materials or biological structures may potentially be described as inversion symmetric crystals that are chiral, offering an alternative to the traditional description of such structures as racemic or containing minimal concentrations of chiral impurities. This possibility can be validated through the calculation of the free energy difference between the left- and right-handed forms of these structures, facilitated by the use of ab initio lattice energy minimization methods in combination with metadynamics for the efficient sampling of the potential energy landscape along the left- to right-handed transition path. This approach can be demonstrated through the study of a model peptide alpha-helical crystalline fragment, for which we calculate the free energy barrier and differences for the left- to right-handed conversion, and identify the relevant metabolic pathways and desymmetrization mechanisms that contribute to the formation of right-handed alpha-helices within the crystal structure. This research can be applied to various left-handed biological structures or chemical components at the molecular scale by providing a quantitative framework for the assessment of the intrinsic handedness

  requirement in various clinical settings.  Our research introduces an ease-to-
  use, low-cost, real-time system for calculating blood oxygen saturation levels
  via a single photodiode from a two-wavelength source.  The device's simple
  design allows for minimized hardware through the use of only one photodiode,
  eliminating the need to account for differences in light intensity across
  different wavelengths.  Our proposed method compensates for this limitation
  via an innovative signal processing technique that utilizes a nonlinear
  decomposition algorithm to break down reflected signals, followed by a
  despread-and-multiply operation to isolate saturation levels.  The method's
  effectiveness was validated through experiments conducted on 24 subjects with
  different oxygen saturation levels, resulting in an average error of 0.38% 
  compared to reference values obtained via conventional dual photodiode method
  or pulse oximetry.  The proposed system was implemented in an FPGA and shows
  real-time processing capabilities at a sampling rate of 100 kHz and an
  estimation period of 200 $\mu$s.  The system's energy efficiency enables the
  continuous non-invasive monitoring of blood oxygen saturation levels in various
  applications across healthcare, sports, and aviation.

  Our investigation focuses on examining the unpredictability of DNNs in
  practice by assessing their consistency on real-world problems. Moving beyond

  Keras using the TensorFlow platform with a range of architectures and

  Our research highlighted several key sources of performance variability,

  aspects of training and inference with modern deep learning software.
  To address the instability of DNNs, we established a framework for reproducibility
  that ensures the consistency of models with respect to critical applications
  specifications, without sacrificing accuracy.

  deep learning, achieving notable improvements of up to 30% in certain cases.

  with regard to output, necessitating future work to address these issues
  in the community. Our methodology has already been utilized in related studies

  metallic with defects. Our study supports the idea that the nickelate
  remains metallic throughout its phase transition, and suggests that
  disorder plays a significant role in driving its surface metal-insulator
  phase transition.

  lines of nitrogen vacancy rows that correlate with the nickelate's
  surface nanodomains and geometric folding, providing a microscopically
  based explanation for the nanoscale coexistence of metal and insulator
  phases that have been observed in other studies.

Our research focuses on modeling the preferences of a decision maker  with multiple objectives in a dynamic environment,  where the attributes of interest subject to constraints do not change. However, the requirement for convertible boolean formulas (CBFs) hinders the full utilization of integer linear programming solvers, as only a fraction of available solvers can convert problem instances to CBFs efficiently.

  This paper presents \emph{Scout}, a specialized tool dedicated solely to checking first-order logical proofs using integer linear programming without the conversion step.  Scout leverages the power of modern ILP solvers through their API, utilizing advanced features like concurrent cutting plane addition and interior-point methods, and can handle convertible-free constraints with disjunctions, negations, and concatenations.

  Theoretical analysis along with experimental results on hard test cases demonstrate the efficiency of Scout, showing that it outperforms even the most capable convertible-producing ILP solvers by significant margins.  Our findings include a critical insight that certain state-of-the-art solvers, after re-branching, can efficiently find the solution without converting to CBFs.  As a result, we recommend using Scout as a precursor to try convertible-producing ILP solvers, and only resorting to them if Scout fails to verify the proof after a reasonable time limit.  Our evaluation indicates that this two-tiered approach leads to a notable number of previously unsolved cases.}, We highlight Scout's key features, a theoretical analysis of its time complexity, and provide the tool itself for adoption by the logical computing community without any hurdles. This generator, named tps-tool, can be utilized to prepare non-convertible integer linear programming instances for evaluation.  Our goal is to promote active collaboration towards developing even more efficient specialized tools for the broad class of computational logic problems without the conversion constraint.  As evidence of this collaboration, we also present a research problem related to Scout: enhancing its memory efficiency for handling large-scale proof checking tasks. A key   distinction it draws from Turing computability involves the capacity   to infinitely iterate primitive functions. We believe this feature warrants   further exploration of nested recursive functions within the dynamic   complexity framework. Specifically, we aim to establish whether it is possible   to determine the dynamic complexity of a function like $f(x,y,z) = z +   x(y^{z})$. This function, representing an infinite iteration of the   unary function $y$, is both primitive and self-referential, making it   an intriguing example to study under the dynamics of recursive functions.   We demonstrate that establishing an upper bound for the dynamic complexity   of $f$ is equivalent to resolving a related issue for partially recursive   functions, which in itself is a challenging problem we have difficulties   solving. However, we do have an uncomputability result arising from our   analysis, which we call the {\em Cantor-Thue-Petrov problem}. This   result itself is derived from a more general, undecidability-like property   we term {\em partial universality}, indicating that a function like $f$   has unbounded dynamic complexity whenever it is injective and maps   integers to integers. This property we believe is significant enough to   be noted on its own. This research was partially inspired by a similar,   though more restricted example of Thue's sequence, which appears in   the famous Thue-Siegel sequence problem, known for its difficulties in   generalizing either Rohlins theorem or the pigeonhole principle within   it. This research of ours also extends the partially universal property to   a class of functions that are Turing reducible, though it highlights the   challenges in using this property in combination with other logical   operators. This research of ours on the Cantor-Thue-Petrov problem can be   seen as a form of diagonalization, which in itself is a form of the   halting problem for partially recursive functions when given an $n$-ary   function and $n$ arguments. This halting problem for partially recursive   functions we believe is another difficult problem to solve. This research of   ours was influenced by a result of R. In the model, this relationship is captured by an exponential function, where the probability of a galaxy spending a given period in a specific environment is directly proportional to the time it spends in that environment, with the proportionality constant varying depending on the environment's mass. By incorporating hierarchical clustering, we can predict the probability of galaxy residence times across a wide range of mass scales, from the most massive clusters to the most isolated dark matter halos. This model enables us to re-examine and refine previous findings related to galaxy migration, specifically the well-known Parkers law, which describes the distribution of residence times for galaxies within a particular mass range. Furthermore, we discovered a fundamental scaling law that governs galaxy residence times across diverse mass ranges, and our analysis shows that this law can be explained by a hierarchical clustering model. This model, in turn, is dictated by a simple rule where more massive systems are composed of several smaller systems that have nearly independent interactions with each other. We validated our model's predictions using outcomes from simulations that deviate from this rule and our results show that these deviations are responsible for the deviations from the predicted residence times for galaxies. A key challenge of the VOF approach is the correct reconstruction of the volume fraction in non-conforming interfaces, which has been addressed in this research by introducing two interface reconstruction algorithms. The first algorithm utilizes a streamwise linearity assumption to calculate the average volume fraction at interfacial nodes, which has been proven to satisfy conservation properties. However, it can introduce numerical diffusion and errors in areas away from the simulation domain boundary. To overcome these limitations, the second algorithm modifies the first-order approach by incorporating adjacent face values in a weighted manner, which has been shown to preserve the continuity of the volume fraction function and reduce numerical diffusion effects. These reconstruction methods have been numerically validated by solving a partial differential equation in a controlled one-dimensional setup. Furthermore, their performance has been assessed in two distinct multiphase test cases – an air pocket breaking through a solid obstacle submerged in a liquid and the flow of a compressible gas through a narrow aperture within a compressible liquid. These simulations demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed algorithms in maintaining interface smoothness and confirm their applicability to both free and forced interface adhesion scenarios. In addition, the results obtained using the second algorithm are found to yield higher Reynolds numbers compared to the first algorithm due to its reduced numerical dissipation. Nevertheless, the performance of the algorithms depends on the chosen mesh size and may require further optimization for complex, free surface simulations. In Poland, where the climate can cause significant snow and frost, these conditions may intentionally or unintentionally cause face and number plate enhancements to become degraded.  With this potential issue in mind, we designed an assessment to evaluate the resilience of DNNs to Polish winter conditions by testing them on face and vehicle license plate recognition.  With the assistance of local authorities, we gathered images in crisp weather along with photos captured in snowy and icy conditions, including those taken at a distance similar to what is typically encountered in Poland.  These images were utilized in three tests: initial, with images captured in the same weather as the models were trained on, and two with snow and frost, captured either mechanically or by a person.  The tests were carried out at various distances.  The DNNs were resistant to snow but struggled with frost.  At the standard evaluation angle and distance, they accurately identified over 90% of faces and over 95% of license plates, even in snow, but with frost, this figure dropped to around 70% for faces and 85% for license plates.  The assessment showed that while DNNs work well in the extreme snow conditions of Poland, they require improvement for functioning properly in the face of frost.)  The DNNs worked best with wide angle shots and shots taken from the side.  The assessment also revealed that training the models on Polish winter images could enhance their resilience to these conditions. This phenomenon arises when a theory exhibits non-perturbative confinement and chiral symmetry breaking due to an almost massless fermion flavor, and it becomes evident through the emergence of anomalous dimensions in the infrared region. Consequentially, the intrinsic cutoff in models mimicking the behavior of such a theory will reflect the non-trivial dynamics of the original theory and can be determined by the degree of chiral symmetry breaking. Comparing genomes of the same species across different ages can provide valuable insights into genomic evolution, but determining the ancient functional meaning of ancient conserved non-coding single nucleotide polymorphisms (csNP) remains difficult due to limited information available from young species genomes.  Since young species retain little genetic diversity, many essential csNPs may have already been lost, obscuring their original functions.  However, the genetic diversity present in the bank cypress species *Salix helvola* offers a unique opportunity to explore ancient csNPs that regulated gene expression along the species's evolutionary path. (MAGICh) experiment was carried
  out at the Baksan Deep Underground Scintillation Array (ND) between 2008 and
  2011. This observatory, located near the village of Seligdar in Dagestan,
  Russia, has a detection sensitivity to very high energy gamma radiation but
  lacks information on the energy and number of particles in air showers, which
  are essential for distinguishing gamma rays from hadronic cosmic rays. To resolve
  this limitation, the MAGICh experiment used radio signals from the shower
  atmosphere, recorded at multiple locations, to determine the energy and number
  of particles in the shower. This approach allowed for identifying gamma-ray
  showers, the separation of air showers by their primary particle type, and
  calculations of the total energy released by cosmic rays in the atmosphere.
  During the experiment, a total of 25 gamma-ray air showers were detected at
  energies above 10^18 eV, with energies ranging from 10^18 to 10^19 eV and
  densities of particles varying from 10 to 10^3 particles per square centimeter
  per second. A crucial feature of the analysis involves removing false positives
  that could arise from extremely energetic hadronic cosmic rays with unusual
  properties, such as large hill-like shapes that might be produced by extremely
  energetic cosmic rays with unusual shapes, such as the "Millipede" event
  reported earlier. To distinguish gamma-ray air showers from hadronic cosmic rays
  with similar energies and particle densities, a threshold was established at
  a maximum particle density of 10^3 particles per square centimeter per second,
  above which the probability of having a "Millipede"-like event is highly unlikely
  and is expected to occur less than once per century for any experiment with
  a similar sensitivity at energies above 10^18 eV. The energy of the 25 gamma-ray

  3.67±0.17, which is consistent with the energy spectra measured by other experiments

  to resist changes in shape through flow when subjected to shear stress. Both
  phenomena become damaged during the cyclic loading process, specifically

COVID-19 pandemic began, healthcare systems around the world have had to tackle a significant increase in severe cornonavirus cases, leading to a corresponding rise in demand for intensive care units, particularly mechanical ventilators. As a result, doctors and healthcare professionals have had to make difficult life-or-death decisions about patients who are critically ill but have the potential to recover with the right treatment. In order to make these high-stakes decisions more manageable, researchers have looked for ways to model lung infection progression dynamically. Consequently, a new dynamic optimization model has been developed to guide treatment strategies for patients with the coronavirus by accurately reflecting lung infection progression on a mechanical ventilator. The model assumes that lung infection progression can be represented as a stochastic control problem with a random initial condition, where the state variable represents the level of lung infection, and the control state represents fluid volume in the lungs. The model's objective is to minimize the risk of death by optimally adjusting fluid volume in the lungs through chest drainage. The authors of the model used optimal control theory to develop a solution, which in turn led to a characterization of an optimal control policy that aligns with chest drainage therapy as proposed by Dr. Cameron. The results obtained from the model have been compared to those from an existing discrete-time model. The researchers behind the model also conducted a set of simulations to demonstrate its potential practical applications. The research presented here is of value to healthcare professionals who can use the model to guide treatment strategies for patients with the coronavirus by accurately reflecting lung infection progression on a mechanical ventilator. The authors of the model plan to continue refining it to make it more practical and user-friendly for healthcare professionals in their daily work. The model developed has potential applications in modeling other types of infections and can be adapted to do so. The researchers behind the model believe that by working together with healthcare professionals, they can make meaningful progress in refining the model and finding practical uses for it in saving lives. The model's numerical implementation is available on the MATLAB Central Repository[2]. The code provided can be used to implement the model presented in the paper "A Stochastic Control Approach to Guiding Chest Drainage Therapy for COVID-19 Patients" [3]. The research presented here is an extension of the paper "A Stochastic Control Approach to Guiding Chest Drainage Therapy for COVID-19 Patients" [3] that was discussed in the webinar "Modeling and Analysis of the Pulmonary Infection Dynamics in COVID-19 Patient under Mechanical Ventilation" [4].   widely present in nature, giving rise to complex behaviors and patterns in
  systems comprising multiple interlinked circular processes. These systems, found
  in the natural world, including the spinning grains, chemical waves, and brain
  activity, among other phenomena, can exhibit captivating, often randomized
  patterns. Our study focuses on a specific category of coupled circular systems
  – rotationally driven rings filled with randomly moving points – and investigates
  their underlying dynamics by observing the movement of individual points within
  the system. Using a two-dimensional Rayleigh-Benard convection model as a
  visual representation, we observe and analyze the collective circular currents
  associated with a system comprising multiple interlinked circles through the
  movement of both the fluid's surface and the distribution of vorticity.
  Notably, we discovered distinct stable states associated with different driving
  speeds and the degree of point movement, and found that even when the point
  movement appears randomized, the system's dynamics can actually be determined
  based on a set of coupled rotation equations representing the relationships
  between the system's circular processes and the movement of individual points.
  This discovery gives a precise, theoretical explanation for a phenomenon known
  as the Hadamard effect, where the system's middle section shows increased
  activity, and provides valuable insights into the driving forces shaping the
  dynamics of complex, coupled systems found in nature. Our study also offers a

  light elements, specifically deuterium, whose density should be around 
  10 to the negative 5 times proton density according to standard nucleosynthesis
  predictions. However, determining the density of deuterium directly from the 
  data is challenging due to its simple composition and the need to model the 
  formation of absorption lines in quasistar spectra. Nevertheless, we can 
  derive a rough estimate for the density of deuterium from the CMBR constraint 
  on baryon density, which is around 0.046 times the critical density, after 
  accounting for electron and baryon dark matter annihilation following the CMBR 
  prober's path. This analysis can be extended to include the effects of 
  adiabatic neutrino damping and the reduction of the baryon density in the 
  quasistar's outer layers by mass loss processes like stellar winds and 
  supernova explosions. Nevertheless, even these additional processes cannot 
  lower the estimated deuterium density from 10 to the 4.5 times proton density, 
  a value that correlates with the metallicity of high-redshift star forming 
  galaxies. This finding supports the idea that the metallicity of these 
  galaxies was extremely low until the era of Population III star formation, 
  a time period that should be targeted in future high frequency radio 
  observations. This estimate for deuterium density can also be compared to 
  direct measurements from high-redshift quasistar spectra, a task that will 
  become feasible with the next generation of extremely deep low-frequency 
  radio telescopes. Furthermore, we propose a method to derive the electron 
  neutrino density from the CMBR constraint on baryon density by analyzing 
  the peak wavelength of the Lyman limit in quasistar spectra. This analysis 
  indicates that if the electron neutrino density is sufficient to cause 
  significant adiabatic damping then we should expect to find a correlation 
  between the peak wavelength and the metallicity of high-redshift star 
  forming galaxies, a search that will be conducted with the next generation 
  of low-frequency radio telescopes through the detection of ultracold molecular 
  lines in these galaxies. This will allow us to confirm the validity of 
  Population III star formation as the primary source of heavy element 
  enrichment, and thereby understand the cosmic origins of heavy elements.

The Iwahori--Langlands classification of irreducible representations of $\mathfrak{p}$ is parameterized by certain triples consisting of a nilpotent element, a 1-dimensional representation of the Levi factor, and a Weyl group element. This paper is concerned with extending this framework to the quotient $\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^{\theta}$. Following the approach of Lusang and MacKay, but with key modifications, we define a category of $\mathfrak{p}$-finite functions on the quotient. Within this category, we find a subset consisting of smooth, compactly supported functions. For each such subset, we can define a representation of the Levi factor. Combining these representations with the orbits of the Weyl group action on a specific variety, we obtain the indexed set of representations corresponding to the closure of the orbit associated with a nilpotent element. This set constitutes a complete set of irreducible representations of the quotient $\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^{\theta}$. The relationship between the indices before and after normalization is governed by the Bruhat--Engelbert-Block-Kostka reciprocity law. The paper's main contribution includes proving the theorem on the completeness of this set, as well as its parametrization in line with the Iwahori--Langlands classification, the theorem on the constancy of the dimensions of representations corresponding to orbits under the Weyl group action, the theorem on the coincidence of the indices calculated by the Weyl group versus the fundamental weights, and the theorem on the reciprocity law. The results have implications for the representations of the affine Lie algebra of Cartan type. The paper also includes the solutions to two open problems proposed by Lusang and MacKay. capacity of multilingual machine translation systems compared to their monolingual counterparts remains an open research question. Recent studies have proposed assessing the effectiveness of models for low-resource languages using intermediate-sized evaluation sets. While finding success in predicting the optimal subset of languages with high generalization ability, they reveal a fascinating phenomenon - a class of languages with markedly poor generalization performance. To better comprehend this observation, we propose a categorization framework for languages into three groups based on their generalization ability: high, medium, and low. Then, to gain insights into the proposed schema, we conducted an experiment where we used genetic algorithms to optimize the selection of training languages for a set of test languages. The results showed that the chosen subset reliably indicated languages with high generalization ability when validated, but failed to accurately represent those with medium ability. This prompted us to re-examine the medium group, discovering that it is actually composed of languages with both high and low generalization ability. This observation prompted us to further refine the schema by dividing the medium group into two subcategories: one with high and one with low generalization ability. We believe that our schema provides a useful framework for interpreting models' ability to generalize, and our findings can guide the selection of training languages for positive transfer. Moreover, we found that our initial results could be improved by incorporating metrics that account for models' robustness and ability to generalize, as demonstrated on the medium group with high ability. To assess the effectiveness of models for low-resource languages using intermediate-sized evaluation sets, we used a dataset compiled from previous studies, and our findings showed that this approach successfully identified languages with high generalization ability. However, we discovered that this method may prioritize languages with both high and medium generalization ability over those with actual low ability. To validate the schema with our specific model, we observed that the medium group accounted for the majority of languages, and further analysis revealed that training on a subset of these languages enhances the model's ability to generalize for the test languages with high ability. Furthermore, our results indicated that our model was already proficient in languages with high generalization ability before retraining, and that the actual improvement resulted from the elimination of languages with both medium and low generalization ability during the genetic algorithm optimization. We also examined the schema through the lens of model performance, examining metrics such as paragraph-level BLEU scores, and found that our approach enhances the model's performance for the test languages with high ability without sacrificing performance for languages with both medium and low generalization ability. We believe that our schema provides actionable guidance

We demonstrate that our estimates match the results obtained from linear network models. We achieve this result through a combination of our main approach with the recent results on the rejection sampling algorithm in [Lyudenko, Daumier] and the moment monotone theorem from [Masi, Preferrti, van der Hofstad]. We also discuss the convergence of the stochastic process and provide the conditions under which the probability threshold increases as the network becomes more complex. also known as tracheal dilation, is an underdiagnosed condition with underdeveloped treatment options. Through a comprehensive review of the literature from the past twenty years, this study aims to clarify the definition, clinical presentation, investigation methods, and management strategies for tracheal dilation in the context of chronic respiratory conditions. Tracheal dilation is characterized by abnormally widened airways below the glottis, and its causes can be intrinsic or extrinsic. Intrinsic causes include conditions like tracheomalacia, tracheal stenosis, and tumors, while external causes involve conditions like foreign bodies, acute angle syndrome, and abnormal blood vessels. The clinical presentation can mimic other conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, or pulmonary embolism. The diagnosis is challenging and usually involves advanced imaging techniques like computed tomography, computed tomography angiography, positron emission tomography, or direct visualization during procedures like bronchoscopies. The management strategy depends on the underlying cause, severity, location, and shape of the dilation, and can range from watchful waiting to surgical interventions like tracheoplasty. It is essential for respiratory healthcare professionals to consider tracheal dilation in the differential diagnosis of chronic respiratory conditions to effectively manage this complex and potentially treatable condition.
